data.caption: canbloomstore.com
data.copy:
I drove to a breeder's house in rural Yorkshire six months after Max died. I wasn't there as a vet. I was there as a woman who lost her German Shepherd and wasn't ready to live in a house without one.

The breeder's name was Joan. She'd been breeding German Shepherds for 28 years. Her name came up in every working-dog circle I'd ever been in. "If you want a Shepherd with good hips, you go to Joan." I'd heard it from clients. From colleagues. From the rescue community. Everyone said the same thing: Joan's dogs keep walking.

I pulled into her driveway expecting a kennel operation. What I found was a farmhouse with 6 adult Shepherds lying on the porch in the sun.

I need to tell you what those 6 dogs looked like because it stopped me before I got out of my car.

They were healthy in a way I'd never seen in my own practice. Coats shining. Eyes bright. But it was how they moved. When I closed my car door, all six stood up. No hesitation. No slow rising. No stiff back legs. No sliding on the wood decking.

Six large German Shepherds getting up simultaneously, and it was effortless.

I treat Shepherds every day. I know what a 41-kilogram dog looks like when it tries to stand.

The oldest was 14.

Fourteen years old.

I've been a veterinary surgeon for 10 years. I have never treated a German Shepherd who lived to 14 with fully functioning back legs. The median mobility decline in my practice starts around 7.

This woman had a 14-year-old Shepherd walking down the porch steps looking better than most 5-year-olds I see in my consulting room.

Joan came out. She was maybe 70. Strong. Direct.

She shook my hand and looked at me the way breeders look at people who might take one of their puppies home. Evaluating. Deciding if I was good enough.

We sat on the porch. The 14-year-old, whose name was Ruth, put her head on Joan's foot and went to sleep.

I couldn't help myself.

I forgot I was there to buy a puppy.

I said: "How is that dog 14 and still walking like that?"

Premium brand. 12mg per capsule. Organic.

"How much astaxanthin do you think is reaching

"I don't know... all of it?"

She pulled out her tablet and showed me a diagram.

"When you take astaxanthin orally, your body breaks it down 
in the digestive system. It enters your bloodstream 
and gets distributed systemically—to every organ, 
every tissue, every cell."

"Right, so my skin gets it too."

"Yes. But by the time it reaches your facial skin through 
circulation, the concentration is approximately 10-15% 
of the original dose. The rest went to your heart, liver, 
muscles, brain, eyes..."

12mg oral dose → ~1.2-1.8mg actually reaches facial skin

and body over hours.

the levels shown in clinical studies to reduce wrinkles—
you need direct topical application."

"So just switch to a serum?"

"Not a bottled serum. Those oxidize. The astaxanthin

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.
